regions.name: Middle East
overview: The US–Iran war has become a sustained tanker war in and around the Strait of Hormuz: the US struck three Iranian oil tankers on 5 September and five more on 8 September, and the IRGC answered with ballistic-missile salvos at a US carrier and destroyer near the strait (5 Sep), the al-Azraq base in Jordan (8 Sep) and US bases in Kuwait and the UAE (3 Sep). Commercial Hormuz transit is falling, an oil-spill incident is a live risk, and Oman-mediated 'transit route' talks have produced no ceasefire.

Yemen's civil war has fully reignited and pulled Saudi Arabia back into an active two-way conflict: heavy Houthi–government ground fighting opened on 3 September, the government declared an offensive toward Sanaa on 8 September, the Houthis hit Saudi oil and energy infrastructure at Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran the same day (73 wounded), and Saudi Arabia flew 32-plus airstrikes across northern Yemen on 9 September — the worst fighting since the 2022 truce, with credible Houthi threats to close Bab al-Mandeb.

Israel's northern fronts escalated even as diplomacy advanced: near-daily Israeli strikes on south Lebanon (4–7 Sep, 10-plus killed) followed renewed Hezbollah drone attacks on IDF troops, while Beirut's cabinet formally adopted a Hezbollah-disarmament plan on 5 September over the walkout of its five Shia ministers; Israeli strikes and ground incursions also continued in southern Syria, where Suwayda clashes resumed.

The Palestinian arena kept degrading structurally beneath the regional war: Gaza's nominal ceasefire ground on with the post-truce toll passing roughly 1,350, West Bank settler violence hit record levels with two Palestinians killed near Qusra on 8 September, and Israel's October election campaign sharpened into a referendum on Netanyahu, the hostages and Gaza. Egypt, Libya and Tunisia saw no kinetic incidents but continued negative drift.

countries.name: Gaza
incidents: 5 Sep — Gaza City (al-Tuffah): Israeli airstrikes destroyed the al-Sakhrah commercial complex, wounding about 12.
6 Sep — West of Gaza City: An Israeli drone strike on a civilian car killed a man and his five-year-old daughter and wounded six.
6 Sep — Deir al-Balah: Israeli artillery hit a classroom in a girls' school sheltering displaced families, killing a child.
8 Sep — Khan Younis / Bureij: Israeli strikes levelled homes as the Gaza Health Ministry put the post-ceasefire toll at about 1,352 killed and 4,511 wounded, up from roughly 1,288 a week earlier.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The October 2025 ceasefire holds only nominally and the attritional pattern — near-daily Israeli strikes, periodic special-forces snatch raids and a steadily climbing civilian toll — will continue with no structural change expected; absent a renegotiated enforcement mechanism the toll is likely to cross 1,600–1,800 by December. Principal escalation risks are a botched raid producing Israeli captives or dead, a mass-casualty strike that forces international pressure, or collapse of the Rafah crossing arrangement. Aid access and reconstruction remain nominal. Israel's October election dynamics are the main external variable: a Smotrich–Ben Gvir ultimatum or a government collapse could bring a renewed large-scale operation.

countries.name: Lebanon
incidents: 4 Sep — Kfar Reman: An Israeli airstrike killed three people and wounded more than 23.
5 Sep — Beirut: The cabinet formally approved the LAF plan to dismantle Hezbollah's arsenal, starting south of the Litani; the five Shia ministers walked out before the vote.
5 Sep — Southern Lebanon and the Beqaa: Israel struck five locations in response to an attempted Hezbollah drone strike on IDF troops in the occupied buffer zone.
6 Sep — Nabatieh, Arab Salim and Kfar Reman: Israeli dawn airstrikes killed at least four and wounded about 20.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Two contradictory tracks are now running. Politically, the 5 September cabinet decision is the first formal state commitment to disarmament and gives the Rome and US-mediated process a document to work from; in practice the LAF will move slowly, avoid direct confrontation and frame activity as reassurance rather than enforcement. Militarily, Israel has widened its strike campaign and Hezbollah has resumed drone attacks on troops, so the tit-for-tat in the south is likely to intensify over the quarter, with recurring multi-casualty days and episodic strikes on the Beqaa. Base case: no Israeli withdrawal, no serious disarmament, slow-bleed escalation — with a strike on Beirut's southern suburbs or a Hezbollah attack that kills Israeli soldiers the trigger for a sharper round.

countries.name: Iran
incidents: 3 Sep — Persian Gulf: An Iranian regular-army missile and drone attack hit US bases in Kuwait and the UAE.
5 Sep — Strait of Hormuz: The IRGC fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer near the strait with no hits; the US responded by striking three Iranian oil tankers.

8 Sep — Strait of Hormuz / Jordan: The US struck five more Iranian oil tankers; Iran retaliated against al-Azraq air base in Jordan and said it had hit tankers on an 'unauthorised' Hormuz route and three US-linked vessels.
2 Sep — Tehran: The rial hit a record of about 2.2 million per US dollar amid a second consecutive day of bazaar and trader strikes over the currency collapse.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The war has shifted from periodic strike waves into a sustained maritime war in and around Hormuz, with each US tanker strike answered by IRGC missile salvos at US warships or regional bases. Commercial transit is falling and a tanker-strike oil spill is a live environmental and economic risk. Oman-mediated talks have produced a claimed transit-route understanding but no ceasefire, and Tehran's rhetoric that 'the era of proportionate responses is over' signals a widening target set. Iranian long-range missile reliability appears degraded — ISW estimates roughly a 50% failure rate against Jordan — slightly lowering the odds of a successful direct strike on Israel but not the intent. The UN snapback and nuclear dispute is unresolved. Base case for the quarter: continued naval attrition, intermittent base strikes across the Gulf and Jordan, further rial deterioration and sporadic domestic unrest, with an Omani-brokered Hormuz de-confliction the most plausible off-ramp but not the base case.

countries.name: Yemen
incidents: 3 Sep — Taiz / Al-Jawf / Al-Bayda: Heavy fighting erupted between the Houthis and government forces — a Houthi offensive in Taiz and a government counter-offensive in Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda — the deadliest since the 2022 truce collapsed.
8 Sep — Al-Jawf / Al-Bayda: The Presidential Leadership Council declared an offensive to retake Sanaa, capturing Yatma and advancing on Dhi Na'im.
8 Sep — Saudi Arabia: A Houthi drone and missile barrage on Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran wounded 73 and started fires at oil and energy facilities.
9 Sep — Marib / Al-Jawf / Taiz / Hodeidah: Houthi media reported 32 Saudi airstrikes as Yemen's UN envoy warned of a wider war and the Houthis threatened to close Bab al-Mandeb.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The civil war has fully reignited and the roughly eight-day post-24 August lull is over. Expect sustained ground combat along the Marib–Al-Jawf–Al-Bayda and Taiz axes, a slow and probably stalling government push toward Sanaa, and continued Houthi long-range strikes on Saudi infrastructure as their primary coercive tool now that the naval blockade has failed to coerce Riyadh. Bab al-Mandeb closure threats are credible enough to keep insurance and rerouting pressure high, and a renewed campaign against Red Sea commercial shipping is likely within the quarter. Humanitarian conditions will deteriorate sharply, and a Saudi ground offensive is now materially more probable given direct attacks on the Kingdom.

countries.name: Israel
incidents: 7 Sep — Jerusalem: Protesters gathered at the Prime Minister's Residence to mark the anniversary of the 'Beautiful Six' hostages' deaths, with families pressing the government over the final 13 deceased hostages.

7 Sep — Rosh HaAyin: Gadi Eisenkot launched the Yashar party's Knesset slate, warning Israel is being led 'dangerously,' with polls putting the coalition below 61 seats and elections expected in October.

8 Sep — Qusra area, West Bank: Israeli troops shot dead a Palestinian during a settler raid on the village and killed another who entered a nearby settler outpost and stabbed and critically wounded a 20-year-old Israeli.
w/o 8 Sep — Jalud, West Bank: A months-long near-daily settler siege of a Palestinian family's home was documented as the UK announced sanctions over settler violence.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. West Bank settler violence has moved from escalating to record levels — the UN calls it an 'all-time high' — with settler–military coordination driving Palestinian displacement in the Nablus and Ramallah hill villages; expect continued weekly killings, at least one mass-mobilisation settler incident and more Western sanctions with little Israeli enforcement change. Domestically the quarter is dominated by an election campaign that is a referendum on Netanyahu, Gaza and the hostages, and a coalition collapse or a Smotrich–Ben Gvir ultimatum is a real risk that could trigger a renewed large-scale Gaza operation. Externally Israel is fighting on the Lebanon and Syria fronts simultaneously and absorbing intermittent Houthi launches at Eilat and the Tel Aviv area; compound-escalation risk is elevated.

countries.name: Iraq
incidents: 2 Sep — Erbil: An IRGC missile and drone strike on a US base destroyed a maintenance centre, warehouses and a surveillance-aerostat guidance system and set fuel tanks ablaze, with reported US casualties.
3 Sep — Iraq: Iran struck US-linked sites in Iraq alongside Bahrain and Jordan after US strikes on Iran.

Through the window — Baghdad: Militia disarmament ahead of the 30 September deadline is in complete deadlock; Kata'ib Hezbollah and Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba tie any disarmament to a US withdrawal, and a Qaani–PM meeting reportedly ended with the Iranian delegation leaving angry.
Early Sep — Iraqi Kurdistan: Unusual US force movements were reported tied to the September coalition-drawdown timeline.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Iraq is now a live front of the US–Iran war rather than a spillover zone. The 30 September disarmament deadline will almost certainly pass unmet; the realistic outcomes are a face-saving nominal handover, a quiet indefinite extension, or — lower probability but rising — intra-Shia armed confrontation if Baghdad attempts enforcement. Expect continued IRGC and militia strikes on US and Kurdish targets in Erbil and on bases, US and Israeli strikes on militia infrastructure in response, and KRG leadership remaining an explicit Iranian target set. The coalition drawdown from Kurdistan proceeding on schedule amid active hostilities is a specific instability risk for the fourth quarter.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
incidents: 8 Sep — Abha / Khamis Mushait / Jazan / Najran: A major Houthi drone and missile attack on southern Saudi Arabia wounded 73, including women and children, and started fires at oil and energy facilities, halting operations at some sites; the Saudi-led coalition vowed a 'resolute response.'
9 Sep — Northern Yemen: Saudi and Houthi sources reported 32 Saudi airstrikes on Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeidah.
Through the window — Yemen: Weeks of escalating government–Houthi clashes shattered the four-year truce, with ISW assessing the Houthis have deliberately shifted to targeting Saudi oil facilities.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The lull is over and Saudi Arabia is back in an active two-way war with the Houthis — absorbing strikes on southern oil and energy infrastructure and conducting sustained airstrikes across northern Yemen. Expect repeated Houthi long-range attacks on Abha, Jazan and Najran and possibly deeper toward eastern Aramco facilities over the quarter, sustained upward pressure on Brent, and continued build-out of the Jeddah maritime coalition. A Saudi ground offensive into Yemen is now materially more likely. The escalation ceiling is a mass-casualty or major-production-loss strike on core Aramco assets, which would be a global oil-market event.

countries.name: Syria
incidents: 1 Sep — As-Suwayda: Clashes coincided with student protests, wounding about 10 Syrian security personnel.
6–7 Sep — West of As-Suwayda: Intermittent clashes resumed between government forces and Hijri-aligned Druze armed groups, killing two civilians.
Early Sep — Rural Suwayda: Four Syrian internal-security personnel were wounded confronting 'outlaw groups.'

Late Aug – early Sep — Quneitra / western Damascus countryside: Israeli artillery shelling near Beit Jinn and ground incursions near al-Rafid continued; the US Syria envoy publicly criticised the strikes.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The Suwayda ceasefire is functionally broken again, with Hijri-aligned Druze factions demanding autonomy and repeatedly clashing with government forces; expect recurring low-level fighting and periodic spikes, with Suwayda remaining outside effective Damascus control through the quarter. The SDF dissolution and army-integration process continues on paper, but Suwayda is the visible proof of the state's weak writ. Israeli strikes and incursions in the south-west will continue as a declared buffer policy, and the unresolved Israel–Turkey standoff over Syrian airbases remains the main wider-escalation risk. Sharaa-government consolidation is slow and contested.

countries.name: Egypt
incidents: No kinetic incident occurred on Egyptian soil in the window.
2 Sep — Cairo: Xi Jinping met President Sisi on his first Egypt visit in a decade and called for a new regional security framework.
Through the window — Suez Canal: Transits and revenue remained roughly 50–60% below normal because of the Red Sea and Hormuz conflicts, with North Sinai still a closed military zone.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Genuinely quiet week on security; Egypt's exposure is indirect. Suez Canal revenue loss is a serious and worsening fiscal drag with no relief in sight while the Red Sea and Yemen fronts are hot, and the Xi–Sisi engagement signals Cairo hedging toward Beijing on both economics and security architecture. The main risks are spillover from a Gaza escalation into Rafah and Sinai, a stray missile or drone during a Hormuz–Red Sea exchange, or renewed Houthi targeting of Bab al-Mandeb traffic that further chokes the canal. The base case is continued heightened alert around the canal and the Sumed pipeline without a direct strike; a second attack on Egyptian soil would warrant immediate re-elevation.

countries.name: Jordan
incidents: 3 Sep — Jordan: Iranian strikes hit Jordanian territory alongside Bahrain and Iraq after US strikes on Iran.

8 Sep — Al-Azraq (Muwaffaq Salti) air base: Iran fired a wave of about 10 ballistic missiles at the base in retaliation for the US strike on five Iranian tankers; Jordanian and US air defences engaged and Jordan said airspace stayed fully open.
Through the window — Jordanian airspace: ISW noted a roughly 50% failure rate on Iranian ballistic missiles fired at Jordan, suggesting degraded Iranian long-range capability.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Jordanian territory is now a recurring impact zone in the US–Iran war — its bases host US drones and Patriot batteries and are being targeted roughly weekly. Amman is deliberately keeping airspace open and downplaying disruption to protect aviation revenue and avoid the appearance of co-belligerency, but debris, intercepts and the risk of a missile getting through are constant. Base case: continued periodic Iranian salvos as long as the US tanker campaign runs, no Jordanian retaliation, and managed but real economic and political strain. The main escalation trigger is an Iranian missile causing significant Jordanian civilian casualties, which would force a harder posture.

countries.name: Libya
incidents: No verified kinetic incident occurred in the window.
~7 Sep — Tripoli: Reporting described a significant militia buildup in the capital, raising fears of imminent armed clashes.

Late Aug – early Sep — Tripoli: A UNSMIL-backed outline agreement was reached for presidential and parliamentary elections within about 24 months under a single executive, with power-sharing under discussion.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained, trending toward the top of the band. There is no active front, but the Tripoli militia rivalry is the live risk — the capital has a history of sudden multi-day armed clashes over institutional appointments and turf, and the current buildup fits that pattern. The new UNSMIL election framework is a modestly positive signal but does not resolve the east–west institutional split or the GNU–GNS deadlock, and disputes over oil revenue and Central Bank control remain a recurring trigger for blockades. Base case: continued brittle stalemate with a roughly one-in-three chance over the quarter of a short, sharp Tripoli clash that would justify an upgrade to HIGH.

countries.name: Tunisia
incidents: 1 Sep — Nationwide: Protests marked five years since President Saied's power grab as older grievances resurfaced.
8 Sep — Tunis: Journalists and activists protested outside a court over the prosecution of prominent journalist Mohamed Yousfi on charges widely seen as fabricated — a new press-freedom flashpoint.
Through the window — Nationwide: Localised protests over water and power cuts and environmental grievances continued, broadening unrest beyond anti-Saied politics into cost-of-living hardship.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. No security escalation; the trajectory is slow authoritarian consolidation with a widening protest base. Expect the monthly anti-Saied demonstrations to continue and grow modestly as post-heatwave service failures compound political grievances, and the crackdown on journalists, opposition figures and civil society to intensify. Economic fragility — the IMF standoff, subsidy pressure and migration politics — is the structural risk. Unrest stays below the threshold of regime-threatening mobilisation in the near term, but the combination of livelihood protests and elite repression is the classic Tunisian pre-crisis pattern and warrants close watching.

regions.name: Ukraine/Russia
overview: Diplomacy without a pause: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner shuttled from Moscow (5 Sep) to Kyiv (6 Sep), both sides briefly halted strikes on each other's capitals from 5–7 September, and then Russia resumed on 8 September. 'Substantive progress' and possible late-September trilateral talks were claimed, but there is no ceasefire and Moscow's Donbas and NATO demands stand.

The pre-winter grid campaign is now live: Russia hit Kyiv and Odesa hard on 8–9 September (more than 17 killed over two days, a TV building struck mid-broadcast) and struck Naftogaz facilities 13 times in a week, shifting to harder-to-intercept jet-powered drones — the energy campaign ISW forecast has begun against thinning Ukrainian interceptor stocks.

Ukraine's deep-strike campaign escalated in range and frequency: strikes hit Sochi (3 Sep), the Ryazan refinery and Rostov airfield and air defences (5–6 Sep), the Salavat petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan some 1,300 km from the border (7 Sep) and the Novorossiysk naval base and oil terminal (9 Sep); Russian refining is stuck near a 20-year low with fuel rationing in a majority of regions.

Twin political stress tests: Russia holds its first wartime State Duma elections on 18–20 September, including in occupied Ukraine, while in Kyiv the NABU/SAP probe widened to the Prosecutor General's office with 5–6 September raids and a former Presidential Office chief was served suspicion for laundering more than UAH 460 million — the corruption crisis around Zelensky's circle is deepening.

countries.name: Ukraine
incidents: 4 Sep — Kyiv: A Russian drone struck the SBU headquarters in the city centre, injuring five; Zelensky said the strike targeted acting SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad, who was unharmed.
5–7 Sep — Moscow / Kyiv: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner met Putin then Zelensky; a mutual halt on strikes against both capitals held only through 7 September before Russia resumed.

8 Sep — Kyiv / Odesa: A combined strike of 166 drones and 32 cruise missiles plus ballistic and anti-ship missiles killed five and injured more than 30 in Kyiv and hit a live TV broadcast; nationwide five killed and 63 injured.
9 Sep — Kyiv / Odesa / Zaporizhzhia: A 24-storey residential block was hit in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district; nationwide 12 were killed and 66 injured over the day.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, compounding. No ceasefire is likely within the horizon despite the Witkoff–Kushner channel; talks may reconvene in late September but Moscow's maximalist terms are unchanged. Expect Russia to escalate combined drone and missile strikes on Kyiv, Odesa and energy and gas infrastructure through October–December to degrade the grid before winter, using more jet-powered drones and larger salvos against thinning Ukrainian interceptor stocks. Frontline pressure continues around Kostiantynivka–Druzhkivka, the Pokrovsk–Myrnohrad flank and Kupyansk with no operational breakthrough likely, alongside localised Ukrainian counterattacks in Sumy and Dobropillia. The NABU/SAP cases now reaching the Presidential Office and Prosecutor General are the most serious internal-political risk to Zelensky since 2022. Ukraine's deep-strike campaign on refineries and ports will intensify as its principal coercive lever.

countries.name: Russia
incidents: 3 Sep — Sochi: Ukrainian naval and aerial drones hit the seaport, two oil depots and an air-defence site; debris from a separate wave struck an apartment block in Pavlovsky Posad near Moscow.
5–6 Sep — Ryazan / Rostov: Ukrainian drones struck the Ryazan refinery, the Rostov-on-Don airfield and three air-defence assets including a radar and two Pantsir-S1 systems.
7 Sep — Bashkortostan: Ukrainian drones hit the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat refining and petrochemical complex some 1,300 km from the border, starting a fire.
9 Sep — Novorossiysk: Ukrainian drones struck the naval base and an oil terminal, with fires reported.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The fuel crisis is likely to persist into the fourth quarter as Ukrainian strikes outpace repairs — petrol is available at fewer than three in ten stations, rationing spans more than half of 83 regions and refining is near a 20-year low — with the diesel and marine-fuel export ban running to 30 September and possibly beyond. The Kremlin will manage the 18–20 September Duma vote tightly, with a United Russia majority assured and polling planned in occupied Ukraine, Abkhazia and South Ossetia, and may time diplomatic signalling around it. Ukrainian long-range strikes on refineries, oil terminals, Black Sea ports and airfields will continue and probably expand, with sporadic civilian casualties in Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod. There is no change to Russia's war aims or its rejection of a genuine front-line ceasefire.

countries.name: Belarus
incidents: 25 Aug – 10 Sep — Belarus / Russia: A Belarusian air-force operational-tactical exercise ran through the window, with a live-fire phase at Russia's Ashuluk range from 5 September.
1 Sep — Bishkek: Lukashenko attended the SCO summit and held informal talks with Putin, Erdoğan and Pakistan's prime minister.
3 Sep — Regional: The CSTO announced its 'Indestructible Brotherhood' and 'Barrier' exercises for October, involving more than 5,000 personnel; there is no 'Zapad-2026' — Zapad ran in September 2025.

Through ~6 Sep — EU border: 78 drones were recorded in Belarusian airspace since 10 August (76 Russian, two Ukrainian) as Latvia, Lithuania and Poland extended border operations and buffer zones into November.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Belarus remains a facilitation and pressure platform rather than a direct belligerent. Expect the October CSTO drills plus continued smaller Belarusian air-force and readiness activity, sustaining a moderate but non-threatening posture on the Ukrainian and NATO borders, with Russian and occasional Ukrainian drones transiting Belarusian airspace. Hybrid migration pressure on Poland, Lithuania and Latvia stays elevated, with buffer zones extended into November. US-brokered prisoner releases continue toward a target of about 1,000, with roughly 890 still jailed, paired with ongoing domestic repression. Direct Belarusian entry into the war remains low-probability over the horizon.

countries.name: Moldova
incidents: Through the window — Chisinau: The government is expected to let its Gazprom supply contract lapse on 30 September; Chisinau is now supplied via South-East Europe, but Transnistria remains entirely Russian-supplied with the cost billed to state Moldovagaz — a standing lever for a winter destabilisation attempt.
Through the window — Nationwide: Political turbulence persists after the 3 July resignation of PM Alexandru Munteanu amid corruption allegations, which collapsed the government.

Late Aug – early Sep — International press: Reporting continued on a Kremlin goal of 'collapsing NATO and the EU from within,' naming Moldova the priority after Ukraine, with GRU-linked training camps in Serbia and Bosnia for Moldovan recruits.
Through Aug — Transnistria: The Russian troop presence of about 1,500 was unchanged, with no new escalation.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. With the September 2025 parliamentary election won by PAS and no new national vote scheduled, the near-term risk is hybrid and energy-centred rather than kinetic: the 30 September Gazprom cutoff and Transnistria's total dependency create a winter-crisis lever, and Moscow will keep running influence operations, disinformation and proxy-protest funding. Lingering instability from the July government collapse compounds the picture. Transnistria stays a latent lever rather than an active front; kinetic escalation risk remains low but non-trivial, concentrated on any enclave energy or humanitarian crisis Moscow engineers.

countries.name: Georgia
incidents: 3 Sep — Tbilisi: New blackmail and bribery charges advanced against former PM Irakli Garibashvili.
7 Sep — Russia: Former Prosecutor General Otar Partskhaladze, wanted in Georgia and UK-sanctioned, announced he would command a new pro-Russian volunteer unit to fight against Ukraine.
8 Sep — Tbilisi: Former Defence Minister Burchuladze was offered a plea deal amid new bribery charges; continuous Rustaveli Avenue protests passed roughly day 650.

9 Sep — Geneva: 34 countries plus the EU raised Georgia's human-rights record and 'justice concerns' at the UN Human Rights Council as a court upheld multi-year sentences over the Chiatura mine protests.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Georgian Dream will intensify the crackdown ahead of the 4 October local elections — more prosecutions and plea-deal pressure on opposition figures — and there is a credible risk it uses any election-day unrest as a pretext to move against leading opposition parties. The opposition's split over whether to boycott hands Georgian Dream near-total municipal control on low turnout. Daily Rustaveli protests and the weekly Saturday march continue past their first anniversary with routine detentions. Western pressure is growing — the UNHRC statement, a possible extension of the EU visa-suspension mechanism to ordinary passports — but will not shift Georgian Dream behaviour within the horizon. Trajectory: continued drift toward Moscow, deepening civil repression, low kinetic risk.

countries.name: Armenia
incidents: 3 Sep — Regional: Armenia is pushing to break ground on the TRIPP ('Trump Route') corridor and courting Central Asian participation; the Armenia–Azerbaijan treaty remains initialled but unsigned.
4 Sep — Yerevan: A judge was assigned to the criminal case against Catholicos Karekin II and six bishops, deepening the government's confrontation with the Apostolic Church.
8 Sep — Yerevan: Armenia's former army chief renounced his citizenship in protest against the government.
9 Sep — Yerevan: Armenia appealed to the EAEU over Russian restrictions on Armenian products as economic friction with Moscow continued.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Peace-process momentum with Azerbaijan holds — no border fire since the August 2025 Washington summit — and TRIPP planning advances, but signature and ratification still hinge on constitutional change via a 2027 referendum. The dominant risk is domestic: Pashinyan's escalating confrontation with the Apostolic Church and with security-establishment figures could generate unrest heading into the 2026 parliamentary campaign. Economic friction with Russia over EAEU export curbs continues alongside Yerevan's EU-accession pivot, and CSTO relations stay frozen. The threat is driven by internal instability rather than external attack.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
incidents: 3 Sep — Baku: President Aliyev addressed an international mine-action conference, noting more than 13% of Azerbaijani territory is mine- or UXO-affected.
7 Sep — Karabakh: A contractor working on reconstruction was threatened with arrest after requesting payment, amid continued consolidation over reclaimed territory.
9 Sep — Karabakh: Azerbaijan began gold mining in reserves formerly under Armenian control.

Through the window — Baku: Relations with Moscow continued to stabilise on the post-December 2024 compensation track; the option of lifting the arms embargo on Ukraine was held in reserve, not exercised.
countries.coa: Downgraded to MODERATE from HIGH. There were no bilateral incidents with Armenia, no border activity and continued normalisation on both the Armenian and Russian tracks, so residual risk is now diplomatic and domestic rather than kinetic. Expect Baku to keep leveraging its position — hosting a Netanyahu visit, expanding defence-industrial ties with Ukraine, holding the arms-embargo lift as a signal to Moscow rather than exercising it — while continuing domestic repression and resource extraction over reclaimed Karabakh. The level should be revisited and re-elevated if treaty signature stalls or border rhetoric returns.

regions.name: Sahel
overview: Junta consolidation versus jihadist initiative: Mali's JNIM fuel blockade passed its one-year mark on 3 September with no relief corridor, and Niger's post-coup-attempt purge and press crackdown deepened — a newspaper editor was detained on 7 September — while both juntas turn inward and the frontline grievances that fuel the insurgencies go unaddressed; Tillabéri villages were attacked again on 2–3 September.

Sudan's war has become a Kordofan war: RSF drone strikes hit an El Obeid market on 4 September (six killed) and the Um Rawaba courthouse on 8 September (13-plus killed), while SAF took Hamrat al-Wiz (6 Sep) and Jebel Moya (3 Sep) and a 5 September UN Panel of Experts report formally attributed the El Fasher rape-and-killing campaign to RSF command; the El Obeid mass-atrocity risk is undiminished.

The Chad–Sudan border is militarised but was static this week: no new strike inside Chad in the window, but the border including Adré stays closed, the army is on maximum alert and President Déby's retaliation order still stands — one more Sudanese strike could force a direct confrontation.

Nigeria pulls in two directions: a secret three-month government–Boko Haram ceasefire in the north-east, revealed on 7–9 September, contrasts with unabated north-west banditry — Tofa in Sokoto (about 10 killed, some 40 abducted) and Giwa in Kaduna (26 abducted) on 7 September — and an ISWAP reprisal threat around Lake Chad after a commander's killing.

countries.name: Mali
incidents: 3 Sep — Bamako / Kayes / Nioro du Sahel: The JNIM fuel blockade entered its second year with no breakthrough; the capital is still supplied only by military-escorted convoys and more than 300 tankers have been destroyed cumulatively.
Through the window — Kayes and Nioro axes: JNIM convoy interdiction and FAMa and Africa Corps counter-operations continued, though no single incident could be independently dated within the window.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. JNIM's most likely course is to hold the western fuel siege as its primary strategic lever while pairing it with periodic mass-casualty convoy ambushes on the Kayes–Bamako and Nioro axes to keep escort costs unsustainable; a symbolic strike into Bamako itself around the blockade anniversary or a national holiday is plausible. Expect continued FAMa and Africa Corps reliance on airstrikes with associated civilian-harm allegations, and further FLA pressure in the north around Kidal and Gao keeping the army two-fronted. Most dangerous course: the blockade tips Bamako into a governance crisis — sustained blackouts, transport collapse, price-driven unrest — that the junta answers with repression, accelerating elite defection of the kind just seen in Niamey. Watch fuel-queue length, official rationing decrees, school closures and embassy drawdowns.

countries.name: Niger
incidents: 2–3 Sep — Anzourou area, Tillabéri: Coordinated armed raids on Darbani, Diamballa, Namarigoungou and Zibane killed and wounded civilians and looted livestock, with two girls drowning while fleeing.

Through 6–7 Sep — Niamey: The junta's purge and detentions of soldiers and alleged accomplices from the 28–29 August coup attempt continued, with power consolidating around Tiani's Presidential Guard.
7 Sep — Niamey: Ali Soumana, editor of the weekly Le Courrier, was arrested and charged, extending the post-coup-attempt press crackdown.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The junta's most likely path is deeper securitisation: continued detentions across the officer corps, tighter Africa Corps integration into the palace guard, further closure of independent media and no concession on the western frontline. Islamic State Sahel Province and JNIM are likely to exploit the distraction with village massacres, road ambushes and at least one company-scale assault on an isolated base in Tillabéri or Tahoua within the window. Most dangerous course: a second mutiny or a targeted strike against Tiani by aggrieved frontline officers, with Africa Corps drawn into internal fighting — a scenario that would fracture the counter-insurgency and open ground west of Niamey. Watch for named senior-officer arrests, unexplained garrison rotations and 'foiled plot' communiqués.

countries.name: Burkina Faso
incidents: In the window — Nationwide: The near-total blackout on security reporting persisted; no incident could be verified from open sources, and the blackout itself is a deterioration indicator rather than a sign of calm.

Ongoing — North and East: The open JNIM–Islamic State Sahel war in Liptako-Gourma and the sieges of Djibo, Sebba and Titao are assessed to be continuing at prior intensity but are unquantifiable this week.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. JNIM's most likely course is to keep tightening blockades on Djibo, Sebba, Titao and Diapaga, contest the Ouagadougou–Dori and Ouagadougou–Djibo axes, and mount periodic massed assaults on military and VDP posts, each capable of 30–100-plus security-force deaths, while Islamic State Sahel fights JNIM for primacy in the tri-border. The junta will continue mass VDP mobilisation and airstrikes, with recurring civilian-massacre allegations against both sides. Most dangerous course: the fall or negotiated abandonment of Djibo, or a spectacular attack in Ouagadougou, triggering another round of coup-plot claims and purges. With independent verification largely gone, treat sudden refugee-flow increases into Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Togo and Benin, or NGO evacuation notices, as the leading indicators.

countries.name: Sudan
incidents: 3 Sep — Jebel Moya, Sennar state: SAF claimed recapture of the strategic heights from the RSF and allied forces.
4 Sep — El Obeid, North Kordofan: An RSF drone strike on a city marketplace killed six and injured 18.
6 Sep — Hamrat al-Wiz, North Kordofan: SAF and allied forces seized the town from the RSF, tightening a supply corridor toward the capital.
8 Sep — Um Rawaba, North Kordofan: An RSF drone strike on the courthouse at peak hours killed at least 13 and injured 22.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, escalating. The RSF's most likely course is to sustain the drone campaign against El Obeid and surrounding North Kordofan towns — markets, courthouses, power and water nodes, hospitals — to make the city ungovernable ahead of a ground assault, while defending Bara and the western approaches; SAF will keep grinding up the Kordofan corridor town by town and pressing in Sennar and Blue Nile. Most dangerous course: an RSF ground offensive on El Obeid producing an El-Fasher-scale massacre of the roughly 1.3 million people, mostly displaced, sheltering there, with a fresh surge west into Darfur and across into Chad. Kordofan displacement, already above 200,000, and West Darfur outflows of about 18,000 a week into Chad will keep rising. The 5 September UN Panel of Experts findings on El Fasher should be read as an early-warning indicator. No ceasefire is likely in the window.

countries.name: Chad
incidents: In the window — Eastern border: No new cross-border strike or clash inside Chad could be verified; the nationwide military alert declared after the late-August Sudanese strikes remains in force.
Ongoing — Adré and other crossings: Borders with Sudan stay closed and thousands of troops remain deployed along the roughly 1,300-km frontier.

Ongoing — Eastern Chad: Refugee inflow continues toward the roughly one million Sudanese already sheltering in the east, with West Darfur fighting pushing about 18,000 people a week across the border.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Most likely course is a continued high-alert posture without direct retaliation: border closures, diplomatic protest, troop reinforcement and quiet tolerance of RSF logistics through eastern Chad that periodically draws SAF air and drone strikes onto Chadian soil. Renewed Sudanese strikes near Adré, Tiné, Wadi Fira or the Ennedi routes are likely within the window given the density of cross-border RSF resupply. Most dangerous course: a mass-casualty strike on a Chadian town or a refugee concentration that forces Déby to act on the retaliation order, pulling Chad into the war on the SAF's opposing side. Watch for N'Djamena statements naming SAF specifically, army convoy movements east, French advisory-mission announcements and any Chadian air activity near the border.

countries.name: Mauritania
incidents: In the window — Atlantic route: No new mass shipwreck or large rescue was reported.
Ongoing — Nationwide: The EU-backed mass-arrest-and-deportation campaign toward Senegal and Mali continued as background, with rights groups still documenting abuses.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Most likely course is a continuation of the current pattern: Mauritania sustains EU-financed pushbacks and interior sweeps, periodic coastguard mass rescues off Nouadhibou, and recurrent deadly drifts on the Atlantic route as departures displace south toward Senegal and The Gambia, with diplomatic friction with Senegal over expelled nationals simmering. Spillover from Mali's Kayes-region JNIM blockade is the key escalation vector — tanker-driver abductions, refugees and possible JNIM probing of the south-eastern border. Most dangerous course: a single shipwreck with 100-plus dead reigniting scrutiny of the EU deal, or a JNIM incident on Mauritanian soil breaking the group's long-standing tacit non-aggression toward Nouakchott. Watch IOM and UNHCR monthly departure figures and any security activity in Hodh Ech Chargui.

countries.name: Nigeria
incidents: 7 Sep — Tofa, Rabah LGA, Sokoto: Bandits raided the town for about four hours, killing seven to ten or more residents and abducting around 40.
7 Sep — Giwa LGA, Kaduna: Bandit raids on three districts killed two elders, abducted 26 and injured one, with rustled cattle recovered after a firefight.

7 Sep — Pulka, Gwoza LGA, Borno: An ISWAP assault on an Operation Hadin Kai position was repelled with air support; the national security adviser warned of ISWAP reprisals after the killing of senior commander Abubakar Mainok.

7–9 Sep — North-east: Reporting revealed a secret three-month government–Boko Haram ceasefire in effect since June, linked to the release of 360 Ngoshe captives, with a possible 40-day extension under discussion and no public confirmation from Abuja.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Most likely course: the quiet government–Boko Haram (JAS faction) truce holds and is extended, modestly reducing violence around the Mandara mountains and enabling further hostage releases, while ISWAP — outside the deal and now motivated to avenge Mainok — steps up assaults on military bases around Lake Chad, Dikwa, Bama and Gwoza, and north-west bandit networks continue village raids and highway and school abductions across Sokoto, Zamfara, Katsina and Kaduna at current or higher tempo. Plateau and Benue farmer–herder killings will resume with the harvest. Most dangerous course: the secret truce leaks fully and collapses amid political backlash just as ISWAP escalates, or a mass school abduction in the north-west. Watch for official confirmation or denial of the ceasefire, further batch hostage releases and ISWAP claims referencing Mainok.

regions.name: Asia-Pacific
overview: The maritime grey zone stayed dominant but non-kinetic this week: China sustained record Coast Guard and navy presence at Scarborough Shoal, east of Taiwan and the Senkakus, ran five straight days of East China Sea intelligence flights past Japan, and advanced likely early-warning-radar construction on Yagong Island in the Paracels, drawing a formal Vietnamese protest — but 3–10 September produced diplomatic sparring, including a Chinese memo handed to the Philippine defence secretary on stage in Seoul, rather than new ramming or water-cannon incidents.

Myanmar remains the region's deadliest conflict and is intensifying on the rivers: junta airstrikes continued to kill civilians (Ye-U 7 Sep, seven killed; Rakhine jet strikes 3 Sep; Loikaw and Minbu 5 Sep, 11 killed), while the KIA landed a major blow to the Bhamo resupply line with a 2 September Ayeyarwady river ambush that netted more than 100 junta prisoners.

Pakistan's Baloch insurgency hit its highest tempo yet: the BLA claimed 28 operations across 12 districts and 52 personnel killed in the first week of September, including a daylight Frontier Corps convoy ambush at Ziarat Cross on 6 September it says killed 18 soldiers — establishing Balochistan as the region's second major conflict driver alongside Myanmar as Pakistani forces also fight TTP infiltration on the Afghan border.

India's Manipur crisis widened onto a new Naga–Kuki-Zo axis, with village arson in Kangpokpi on 1 September, seven-plus killed in late August and an HRW alarm on 3 September — warranting an upgrade to HIGH. Elsewhere the week was calmer: North Korea marked its founding day on 9 September with no missile activity since 20 August but a deepening troop commitment to Russia, the Thai–Cambodia ceasefire held with a UN conciliation track opening, and Sri Lanka was quiet enough to downgrade to LOW.

countries.name: North Korea
incidents: 2 Sep — Tongchon: Commercial satellite imagery showed the demolition of civilian villages around the Tongchon missile base to enable base expansion.
6 Sep — East Sea: North Korea commissioned the guided-missile destroyer Kang Kon into the East Sea Fleet, with Kim framing the navy's role as 'restraining' adversary fleet deployments.
9 Sep — Pyongyang: A 78th national founding-day ceremony was held with no parade or missile event; the launch streak since the 20 August barrage continues.

3–10 Sep — Russia: Ukrainian military intelligence assessed Kim could be asked for up to about 50,000 additional troops at an expected September Putin–Kim meeting, on top of the roughly 11,000 already in Kursk.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Expect the quiet-on-launches posture to hold through the 10 October party founding anniversary, after which a demonstration launch or satellite attempt becomes more likely as a political marker. The near-term signal to watch is a Kim–Putin meeting and any formalised new troop tranche to Russia, which would harden the axis and could draw a coordinated South Korea–US–Japan response. Naval modernisation and Tongchon air-defence construction indicate continued conventional build-out rather than crisis initiation. US–DPRK diplomatic feelers are a wildcard that could freeze provocations if a leaders' meeting firms up; absent that, treat the founding-day-to-anniversary window as elevated but not acute.

countries.name: Myanmar
incidents: 2 Sep — Ayeyarwady River, Shwegu–Bhamo stretch: KIA joint forces ambushed a junta river flotilla moving toward Bhamo, striking about eight vessels, sinking one and burning another, and claiming more than 100 prisoners.
3 Sep — Rakhine (Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Rathedaung): The junta deployed about four fighter jets against Arakan Army-held areas.
5 Sep — Loikaw / Shadaw / Minbu / Myaing: Junta airstrikes and ground raids killed 11 civilians.

7 Sep — Ye-U Township, Sagaing: Junta gyrocopters and an Mi-35 helicopter struck a vehicle-repair workshop by a village market with no fighting in the area, killing seven civilians and wounding three.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, deteriorating. The junta's civilian-directed air campaign is a fixed feature and will continue at three to four civilian deaths a day in Rakhine plus recurring Sagaing, Magway and Karenni strikes, with periodic mass-casualty events at markets, schools and religious sites. The decisive operational contest is the Bhamo resupply corridor: KIA and PDF interdiction of the Ayeyarwady river route is degrading the junta's ability to sustain its Bhamo garrison, so anticipate intensified junta air support and possible localised withdrawals over the quarter. The military-backed post-election government confers no legitimacy and changes nothing on the ground. Baseline trajectory: continued attritional stalemate with resistance gains in Kachin and northern Shan and sustained junta air dominance.

countries.name: Pakistan
incidents: 1 Sep — Pasni, Gwadar: The BLA opened its September campaign, attacking a joint police and Levies post and coastal checkpoints.
3 Sep — Afghan border opposite North Waziristan: The military said security forces killed 15 militants during an attempted infiltration.
6 Sep — Ziarat Cross, Balochistan: A BLA 'Fateh Squad' ambushed a Frontier Corps convoy in daylight, claiming 18 soldiers killed and two vehicles destroyed.
9 Sep — Balochistan-wide: The BLA claimed 28 operations across 12 districts for 1–7 September with 52 personnel killed, admitting 12 fighters lost.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The BLA has institutionalised a province-wide, multi-district operational tempo with a shift toward large set-piece convoy ambushes rather than only harassment, signalling improved coordination and a manpower base that absorbs losses. Expect this rate to hold or rise through year-end, with Chagai, Pishin, Mastung and Kalat as the hot belt and periodic spectacular attacks on Frontier Corps convoys, rail and Gwadar and CPEC-linked targets. TTP pressure in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and cross-border friction with Afghanistan compound the two-front strain, and Islamabad will likely continue cross-border airstrikes into Afghanistan, raising escalation risk with the Taliban. There is no political off-ramp in Balochistan; AJK grievances remain a secondary flashpoint.

countries.name: India
incidents: 1 Sep — Kangpokpi district, Manipur: Armed groups opened fire and burned about 30 houses in Liangmei Naga villages along the Imphal–Tamenglong road amid Naga–Kuki-Zo fighting.

3 Sep — Manipur: Human Rights Watch issued an alarm over renewed ethnic violence, citing at least seven killed in late August in hill-district clashes, mutual abductions of about 48 people and six Naga hostages found dead.
Context — Manipur: The violence has opened a new Naga–Kuki-Zo axis distinct from the Meitei–Kuki valley–hill fault line; the announced 28 September Kuki-Zo shutdown remains pending.
countries.coa: Upgraded to HIGH from MODERATE. The Manipur conflict is broadening rather than settling: the Naga–Kuki-Zo front along the Kangpokpi and Imphal–Tamenglong corridor adds a new driver on top of the unresolved Meitei–Kuki dispute, and reciprocal abductions raise the risk of tit-for-tat massacres. Expect continued low-level arson, ambushes and road blockades through the quarter, with the 28 September Kuki-Zo shutdown and any central move on statehood or administrative arrangements as escalation triggers; President's Rule and central forces are containing but not resolving the situation. Elsewhere in India — Jammu and Kashmir, the Naxal belt — the week was quiet with no window-specific escalation. The risk of a single high-casualty Manipur incident re-triggering wider valley unrest remains real, with added exposure from Myanmar spillover.

countries.name: China
incidents: 3 Sep — Waters east of Taiwan: The China Coast Guard announced 'routine law-enforcement patrols' on Taiwan's Pacific side, continuing a normalised pattern of continuous cutter presence since June.
3–7 Sep — East China Sea: PLA Y-9 intelligence aircraft operated on five consecutive days, with Japanese fighters scrambling each time and no territorial-airspace violation.
5 Sep — Taiwan ADIZ: Taiwan tracked 20 PLA aircraft sorties, 12 crossing the median line, plus six navy and five official ships.

Late Aug – early Sep — Paracels: Satellite imagery showed a likely early-warning radar facility under construction on Yagong Island with parallel buildup on Antelope Reef; Vietnam lodged a formal protest.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. The sea-over-air rebalancing continues to hold: PLA ADIZ air incursions are down roughly 52% year-on-year while Coast Guard and navy maritime presence is at or above record levels and is being made permanent through continuous patrols east of Taiwan, Scarborough encirclement and Senkaku contiguous-zone presence. Paracel construction is a medium-term ISR and basing upgrade that strengthens Beijing's control of the northern South China Sea and will keep drawing Vietnamese and Philippine protest. Expect the coercion to stay grey-zone and below the use-of-force threshold through the quarter, with elevated risk of an unintended collision at Scarborough or east of Taiwan, and episodic exercise surges tied to Taiwan's November referendum and local elections or a US arms announcement.

countries.name: Taiwan
incidents: 5 Sep — Taiwan Strait / ADIZ: 20 PLA aircraft, six navy and five official ships were tracked, with 12 median-line crossings into the northern, central and south-eastern ADIZ.
7 Sep — Around Taiwan: Taiwan tracked 17 Chinese vessels, 13 of them navy, and two PLA aircraft, all crossing the median line.
1–7 Sep — Around Taiwan: Running September totals reached 26 PLA aircraft and 69 ship tracks.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Cross-strait military pressure remains steady-state at the new normal — continuous naval and Coast Guard presence, routine median-line crossings, lower air tempo. The NT$240 billion drone special budget passed on 27 August and the November nuclear-policy referendum are the domestic markers for the quarter; expect Beijing to time a larger Joint Sword-style exercise to a political trigger such as a Lai speech, a US arms-sale announcement or transit diplomacy. The Nvidia AI-chip smuggling probe and submarine-programme progress continue in the background. Baseline: sustained pressure, no imminent crisis, with collision risk the main tail hazard.

countries.name: Philippines
incidents: 8 Sep — Seoul: Chinese representatives handed Defence Secretary Teodoro a memo asserting Beijing's South China Sea position while he was on stage discussing grey-zone coercion; Teodoro rebuked China publicly.
9 Sep — Beijing: China's foreign ministry accused the Philippines of 'stirring up trouble' in response.

3–10 Sep — West Philippine Sea: No new water-cannon, ramming or collision incident was confirmed at Scarborough or Pag-asa, but sustained Coast Guard and navy encirclement continued, with Philippine vessels reportedly pushed about 40 nautical miles from Scarborough.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The confrontation has stabilised at a high but sub-kinetic level: China maintains near-permanent presence and multiple semi-permanent structures and buoys around Scarborough and heavy deployment near Pag-asa, while Manila's push for a regional 'rulebook' has stalled. Expect resupply runs to Filipino fishermen and to Pag-asa to keep drawing water cannon and close-quarters manoeuvring, with periodic injuries, and the US carrier gap to remain an aggravating factor for at least part of the quarter. A serious collision, or a Chinese move to physically occupy or build at Scarborough, are the escalation scenarios to watch; diplomacy will not change Coast Guard behaviour.

countries.name: South Korea
incidents: 8 Sep — Seoul: At the Seoul Defense Dialogue, Defence Minister Ahn Gyu-back said North Korea is fortifying the DMZ 'beyond precedent' with layered fencing and mines and called for resumed US–DPRK dialogue 'backed by strong deterrence,' hoping for a Trump–Kim meeting.
8–10 Sep — Seoul: The Seoul Defense Dialogue hosted about 1,000 delegates from 67 nations, with the NATO Military Committee chair attending.
Through the window — Seoul: No new North Korean launches; Kimsuky and other DPRK cyber-espionage activity against ministries and defence firms continued.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. The Lee government is consolidating a 'dialogue plus deterrence' line and actively courting a Trump–Kim summit; if that materialises, expect a near-term freeze on peninsula provocations and possibly reciprocal South Korean gestures at the DMZ. Absent a summit, the DPRK founding-day-to-party-anniversary window through 10 October carries elevated launch risk. Domestically the post-31 August cabinet, including a new defence minister, is bedding in at around 40% approval. DPRK cyber operations against South Korean targets will continue regardless of the diplomatic track. Baseline: stable, with upside if summit diplomacy advances.

countries.name: Vietnam
incidents: Late Aug – early Sep — Paracels (Yagong Island): After satellite imagery showed a likely Chinese early-warning radar site under construction, Vietnam's foreign ministry said it 'resolutely opposes' the activity and demanded it stop, sustaining diplomatic protest through the window.
Through the window — Spratlys: The South China Sea was otherwise quiet for Vietnam, with Chinese patrols continuing around Vietnamese-held features.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Hanoi will keep the dispute in the diplomatic-protest lane while continuing its own Spratly reclamation across all 21 held features and deepening the parallel political track with Beijing. Chinese Paracel construction is a strategic irritant, not a near-term clash trigger; expect rhetorical friction and occasional standoffs around oil-and-gas blocks and fishing grounds but no kinetic escalation this quarter. Vietnam continues hedging via defence diplomacy with the US, Japan and the Philippines, historically underreporting maritime incidents when they occur.

countries.name: Japan
incidents: 3–7 Sep — East China Sea: Chinese Y-9 intelligence aircraft operated on five consecutive days, with Japanese fighters scrambling each time and no territorial-airspace incursion.
Through the window — Senkaku Islands: Record-level China Coast Guard presence continued, extending a pattern of near-daily contiguous-zone entries.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained; watch for a possible upgrade given rising rhetorical intensity. Expect continued near-daily Coast Guard contiguous-zone presence at the Senkakus, periodic territorial-sea intrusions and recurring intelligence flights along the south-western approaches prompting Japanese scrambles. The 2026 Defense White Paper framing of China as the 'greatest strategic challenge' locks in the posture, and Japan–China relations remain cold. Escalation risk is low but a fishing-boat incident or an airspace violation could spike tensions quickly, as could a North Korean missile overflight. Baseline: steady pressure, no crisis.

countries.name: Indonesia
incidents: 2 Sep — Mile 60, Tembagapura, Mimika (Central Papua): TPNPB gunmen fired on a 15-vehicle Freeport Indonesia convoy, hitting three vehicles with no casualties; police recovered three 5.56 mm casings.
Through the window — Papua highlands: TNI operations against the TPNPB continued in Puncak Jaya and Intan Jaya following the mid-August drone strikes.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. The TPNPB will keep targeting economic and security infrastructure — Freeport convoys and mining roads, telecom towers, aircraft at highland airstrips — with periodic civilian casualties, while the TNI sustains offensive sweeps and armed-drone strikes in Puncak and Intan Jaya. Expect the tempo to stay elevated through the quarter with no political dialogue track, and a real risk of a mass-casualty event — an ambush of workers or a downed aircraft — that internationalises the issue. The militarised counter-insurgency approach and drone use are drawing human-rights criticism that will grow if civilian tolls rise, and media and monitor access stays highly restricted.

countries.name: Thailand
incidents: 3 Sep — Phnom Penh: Cambodia's defence ministry briefed 22 foreign military attachés on the border situation; the December 2025 ceasefire is holding.
~10 Sep — Announced: Thailand and Cambodia will hold their first meeting under a UN conciliation process on the maritime boundary in Singapore the following week.
Through the window — Border: Land borders remain fully closed since June 2025, with Chanthaburi border-fence friction continuing.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained, with a de-escalation tilt. The ceasefire should hold through the quarter, reinforced by the new UN conciliation process and continued third-party attention. Residual risks are localised clashes around contested temple and land sectors, landmine incidents, and nationalist politics on both sides as Cambodian conscription begins in 2026. The closed land border imposes an ongoing economic and humanitarian cost but is not itself an escalation driver. Trajectory: slow diplomatic thaw, low risk of renewed major fighting.

countries.name: Bangladesh
incidents: 1 Sep — Dhaka: The army chief met the head of government to discuss the military's role assisting civil administration ahead of national elections.
Through the window — Dhaka: July Charter implementation remained deadlocked, and relations with India stayed cold over Sheikh Hasina's continued political activity from Indian soil.
In the window — Nationwide: No significant security incident was reported.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. The transitional political landscape stays fractious — Charter-implementation disputes, Awami League proscription grievances and economic strain — with India relations frozen over Hasina's status and affecting trade, border, water and transit issues. The pre-election period will see rising political-violence risk, heavier military involvement in law and order, and campus and communal unrest; no single flashpoint is likely to breach MODERATE, but cumulative instability is rising. The Bangladesh entry should be reviewed next cycle against the post-transition political timeline.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
incidents: 2 Sep — Maritime: Sri Lankan and US authorities seized about 463 kg of crystal methamphetamine linked to a Pakistan-based trafficking network.
7 Sep — Geneva: A UN human-rights report found little progress on accountability for civil-war-era crimes and enforced disappearances.
9 Sep — Colombo: President Dissanayake assured India that Sri Lankan territory would not be used against Indian security interests, and three defence-cooperation agreements were signed with India.
countries.coa: Downgraded to LOW from MODERATE. This is a second consecutive quiet week: no unrest, stable governance under the NPP, prison unrest contained, and deepening rather than deteriorating ties with India. Expect continued stability, with the main watch items being economic-adjustment protests tied to the IMF programme, the new counter-terrorism law's implementation and its civil-liberties criticism, and the pace of India–Sri Lanka defence cooperation. No indicators point to security deterioration this quarter; review monthly, with a large-scale prison riot or a custodial-death scandal the main risk to the assessment.

regions.name: Americas
overview: The US boat-strike campaign resumed after a roughly two-month pause: a 9 September Caribbean strike killed three, bringing the Operation Southern Spear toll to about 230 across some 70 vessel strikes, and SOUTHCOM's 2 September one-year update framed the operation as ongoing. A strike on or near Venezuelan territory remains the top regional escalation risk.

Venezuela's US-controlled oil model is now the governing reality: the 1 September award of a 100-year concession over 17 oil fields to a US-government-linked partnership, plus Trump ruling out any election timetable on 2 September, is generating sovereignty pushback from Latin American governments and setting up domestic backlash as banks warn price relief is years away.

Explosive-drone and boat-IED warfare is spreading in Colombia: a US Embassy alert for Cesar on 3 September, a roughly 20-drone ELN swarm attack that killed three soldiers at Ocaña on 4–5 September, a Timbiquí boat-IED around 10 September, and emergency counter-drone deployments show the ELN and FARC dissidents escalating against security forces and civilians with no negotiated off-ramp.

Governance and legitimacy clocks are running down in Haiti and Bolivia: Haiti's Gang Suppression Force mandate expires on 30 September with December elections effectively unviable, and Bolivia's state-of-emergency cover has lapsed into a fuel-shortage crisis with Evo Morales mobilising against President Paz. Peru and Ecuador continue governing by rolling emergency decree, and Cuba was quiet enough for a second week to move down a band.

countries.name: Venezuela
incidents: 1 Sep — Caracas: The US-backed interim government awarded a 100-year concession over 17 oil fields to a US-based partnership, with Washington to control about 55% of output.

2 Sep — Washington: A SOUTHCOM one-year update on Operation Southern Spear claimed record maritime-traffic reductions; the same day Trump said Venezuela is 'not ready' for elections and set no timetable.
9 Sep — Caribbean: The US carried out the roughly 70th boat strike of the campaign, killing three and ending an approximately two-month lull; the running toll is about 230 killed.
1 Sep — Maiquetía: Caracas's main international airport reopened with temporary modules two months after the June earthquake, at about 70% capacity.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Overt US–Venezuela military confrontation has settled into a US-backed negotiated transition, but the boat-strike campaign has resumed. Expect it to continue at a low but non-zero tempo of one to two vessel strikes a month rather than return to the late-2025 peak, with a strike on or near Venezuelan territory the principal escalation risk and SOUTHCOM assets remaining offshore as leverage. Politically, the oil-concession model under Delcy Rodríguez is now the governing reality: watch for hardline-Chavista and opposition friction over sovereignty and the absence of an election timetable, regional pushback, and sporadic Caracas protests over prisoners, fuel prices and the concession terms. Investment-bank scepticism that output or price relief is near sets up domestic disappointment; Maduro's US trial, set for June 2027, will periodically re-inflame sovereignty protests.

countries.name: Colombia
incidents: 3 Sep — Cesar department: The US Embassy issued a security alert over an elevated risk of ELN explosive-drone attacks on police and military posts.
4–5 Sep — Ocaña, Norte de Santander: An ELN attack on a military compound using about 20 explosive-laden drones followed by a ground assault killed three soldiers and injured four.
w/c 8 Sep — Cesar: The government announced a 'security shock plan,' deploying counter-drone systems to El Copey, Curumaní, La Jagua de Ibirico, Pelaya and Valledupar.
10 Sep — Timbiquí, Cauca: A boat-borne IED exploded in the town, injuring about eight marines and damaging 100 to 200 homes; attributed to a FARC-dissident faction.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The de la Espriella government's hardline posture and the end of 'Total Peace' mean no negotiated off-ramp; expect the ELN and the FARC dissidents to keep escalating drone-swarm and boat-IED attacks on security forces and civilian infrastructure, concentrated in Cesar and Norte de Santander near the Venezuelan border and along the Cauca and Nariño Pacific coast. Counter-drone deployments will blunt but not stop attacks. Rising civilian harm — Timbiquí displacement, the earlier child-casualty scandal — will drive domestic political pressure and the confinement of Afro-descendant and Indigenous communities. Cross-border ELN sanctuary in Venezuela is a wildcard given the US presence there.

countries.name: Haiti
incidents: 29 Aug – 2 Sep — Petite Rivière de l'Artibonite: Renewed armed-group violence displaced residents from Jean Denis and Pont Benoît, tracked by IOM.
4 Sep — Port-au-Prince: Foreign Minister Raina Forbin formally asked the UN Security Council to renew and fully resource the Gang Suppression Force, whose mandate expires on 30 September.
~8 Sep — Artibonite: Police reported about six alleged gang members killed during a road-clearing operation.
Ongoing — Kenscoff: Fallout from the 23–24 August massacre continued, with hostage releases and metro-area displacement still climbing.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, worsening. The 30 September Gang Suppression Force mandate expiry is the pivot point: a lapse or an under-funded renewal would remove the only external check on Viv Ansanm as gangs consolidate control of roughly 90% of the capital and push into five or more departments, Artibonite especially. Expect continued gang offensives on previously safe communes, mass abductions, and rising civilian casualties from police drone strikes. The 13 December elections are almost certainly not deliverable nationwide; watch for an official postponement that deepens the legitimacy crisis of the transitional authorities. Humanitarian access is shrinking.

countries.name: Cuba
incidents: 28 Aug – 10 Sep — Nationwide: No further national grid collapse was recorded, with the island still on prolonged localised blackouts of 12 to 20-plus hours a day in the provinces.
Late Aug – early Sep — Havana and other cities: Sporadic localised blackout protests continued and were dispersed quickly by state security.
20 Aug — Washington: Fresh US sanctions on 10 Cuban state firms continued to accelerate foreign-firm withdrawal.
countries.coa: Downgraded to HIGH from CRITICAL. No acute event occurred in the window and the acute grid-collapse phase has passed, though systemic fragility — any of eight ageing thermal plants failing can trigger a cascade — still justifies HIGH. Base case is continued rolling blackouts, periodic localised protests dispersed quickly, and a low but real probability of another full national grid collapse, especially through hurricane season. Economic contraction and migration outflow continue, and US sanctions pressure is unlikely to ease. A large-scale protest event on the scale of July 2021 remains the low-probability, high-impact scenario, most likely triggered by a multi-day total blackout in Havana during peak heat — which would warrant immediate re-elevation.

countries.name: Ecuador
incidents: 3–10 Sep — Nationwide: The window was quiet on headline incidents; the state of emergency continued across about 10 provinces with homicide rates at record levels.
Ongoing — Guayas / Los Ríos / Manabí / Esmeraldas: Organised-crime violence and prison tension persisted alongside deepening US security cooperation at Manta and Esmeraldas.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, driven by the sustained homicide and organised-crime baseline rather than a new event. Expect continued state-of-emergency renewals, high homicide rates concentrated in the coastal provinces and the northern border, periodic prison massacres between Los Choneros and Los Lobos, and a persistent risk of urban IED attacks in Guayaquil tied to government anti-gang operations. US cooperation deepens through basing and interdiction, and further publicised joint operations and possible US strikes on vessels off Ecuador's Pacific coast are likely. Fuel-subsidy tensions are a protest driver layered on top of the security crisis.

countries.name: Peru
incidents: 5 Sep — Junín / Cusco / Ayacucho and other regions: Sweeping states of emergency were declared across 17 districts amid an extortion surge, plus crackdowns in Piura.
6 Sep — Nationwide: A supreme decree imposed a 60-day state of emergency covering five high-security prisons to disrupt extortion rings run from cells.
Ongoing — Nationwide: The El Niño 60-day emergency across about 893 districts continued, with transport-sector extortion and strike threats persisting under the Jerí government.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Extortion-driven violence — record case volumes, attacks on transport and small business — will keep forcing the Jerí government into reactive emergency decrees with limited effect. Expect further prison-focused measures, possible military deployment to Lima, Callao and Trujillo, and recurring 24-to-48-hour transport strikes, with El Niño flooding and landslide impacts compounding through the rainy season. The 2 September rupture of ties with Iran is largely symbolic for domestic security. Political instability under a weak executive remains a background risk.

countries.name: Bolivia
incidents: 1 Sep — La Paz: The government took emergency control of state oil firm YPFB's fuel imports for up to 180 days amid worsening diesel and gasoline shortages.
Late Aug – early Sep — Beni: Producers blocked the San Pablo bridge east of Trinidad demanding repeal of the decree that ended subsidised diesel for large consumers.
9 Sep — Nationwide: The US Embassy warned of planned protests and road blockades as the 20 June state of emergency lapsed and Evo Morales mobilised supporters for marches toward La Paz.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Fuel scarcity is now the dominant driver: as the state-of-emergency cover expires, expect a fresh wave of blockades by transporters, farmers and Morales-aligned groups through October, with the government using the military to clear roads reactively. Morales's push for President Paz's resignation and the suspension of his own prosecution keeps a destabilisation campaign live, and diesel-subsidy cuts will keep generating rural unrest. The risk of a renewed nationwide blockade crisis comparable to May and June is moderate-to-high, with reserves and inflation the deciding variables; a de-escalation to MODERATE is defensible only once the October window passes without major unrest.

countries.name: Dominican Republic
incidents: 3 Sep — Santo Domingo: The Dominican Republic and Haiti signed a border-cooperation pact; within days the government broke ground on a new border-wall section and detained 58 Haitians.
Early Sep — Nationwide: The migration authority logged 35,276 Haitian deportations in August, the highest single-month figure of 2026.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. Expect the roughly 1,000-a-day expulsion pace to hold or rise, continued border-wall construction, and periodic small detention sweeps. Friction points are international rights criticism over statelessness and racial profiling, possible Haitian-government protest despite the pact, and localised border incidents, with the arrival of US TPS-termination deportees adding pressure. Internal stability is solid; the principal risk is a border clash or a mass-casualty incident during an expulsion operation, and continued rights-group documentation of detention conditions as the main reputational risk.

countries.name: Jamaica
incidents: ~5–6 Sep — Bull Bay, St Andrew: Police killed a suspect linked to a string of murders.
8–9 Sep — Watson Grove, Portmore: Police fatally shot two men in an intelligence-led operation; INDECOM was notified.
9 Sep — Mount Salem, Montego Bay: A gunfight left three police officers wounded and a wanted man dead.
9–10 Sep — Robins Bay, St Mary: Gunmen fired into a bar, killing three including the owner and a bystander.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. The 2026 homicide decline — still tracking roughly 40% below 2024 — is likely to hold into year-end, supported by continued state-of-emergency-style operations, though clusters in St James, St Catherine and St Mary will persist and multiple-victim shootings will continue to draw attention. Watch the INDECOM caseload from the rise in police-involved killings this week: a controversial incident could generate political and oversight friction. Bushfire and drought conditions are a secondary strain on emergency services, and peak Atlantic hurricane season in September and October is the more material near-term risk to stability.
